newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fireworks, bagpipes herald 1997 in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Fireworks, bagpipes herald 1997 in Hong Kong.

text.p: Fireworks painted the night sky red as Hong Kong saw in 1997, the year when the wealthy British colony is destined, like it or not, to become part of China again.

Bagpipes skirled, car drivers pounded their horns and teenagers screamed a welcome to a year when more than 150 years of British rule ends at midnight on June 30 and the red flag of China rises over this wealthy community.
While the world marked just another countdown on the road to the next millennium, Hong Kong contemplated the change ahead.
For the colony's 6.3 million people, 1997 is branded in the collective memory as shorthand for the handover to Communist China in 181 day's time.
For a few hours, hedonism triumphed, reinforced by the fizz of champagne bubbles and the crack of fireworks, relegating concerns about the future to the backburner.
Hong Kong's post-handover leader, Tung Chee-hwa, urged the community to stand "united together to build a better tomorrow".
China's President Jiang Zemin heralded the impending return of Hong Kong as "washing away a century of disgrace".

Scottish ghosts of the founders of the Jardine Matheson trading empire, who urged the British government into the Opium Wars with China leading to the seizure of Hong Kong in 1841, were recalled when the Jardine gun boomed out at midnight.

The Jardine gun has a special place in Hong Kong history. Early Jardine merchant princes fired a military-style salute to mark the arrival of the company chairmain aboard a tea clipper in the last century, to the ire of the British military.
Their punishment was to mark every noon with gunfire -- a custom seized on by the founders' descendants who to this day signal every noon with cannon fire.
"Of course it will continue," said a Jardine official referring to beyond the transition. "Why not?"
Foreign eyes grew misty as Hong Kong's once influential Scottish expatriates saluted the eerie notes of Auld Lang Syne from a lone piper floating out across the sea.
But the wail of bagpipes failed to blot the undercurrent of concern. Outside Hong Kong's Legislative Council, pro-democracy politicians congregated to vow no surrender.
They counted down the seconds to the New Year and pledged to do battle against what they regard as efforts by Beijing to roll back freedoms and democracy.
"Keep my seat warm," shouted Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's largest party, the Democracy Party, which is due to be kicked out of the Legislative Council at the handover.

China aims to dissolve the elected legislature and replace it with an appointed body when it takes over next July 1, undoing electoral reforms spearheaded by the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, passed in the twilight of British rule.
A small but vocal group of demonstrators gathered outside the offices of China's de facto representative office in Hong Kong demanding the release of dissidents jailed by Beijing.

In Hong Kong's nightclub district, police threw a tight but low-key cordon around the popular quarter of Lan Kwai Fong, scene of a 1992 New Year tragedy when almost two dozen young revellers were crushed to death on the slippery slopes as crowds got out of hand.
"Happy New Year," bubbled a shaven-headed British teenager to a leather-clad Chinese rocker as she offered him a sip from her bottle of sparkling Australian wine.
